cells.tense: You are steady right now, and none of it is performance.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you carry for them, then let them take something off your hands this week.
cells.core:
You're holding what the hard stretch left you with, and your grip is easy. Not braced, not clenched — it stands on its own, and you know that. People lean on you and you don't buckle, and it isn't costing you anything you'd rather keep.

What keeps this clean is that it moves both directions. You hand back what you get, roughly, without a ledger. One thing is worth checking: whether you let the return come in as often as the offer goes out. If staying solid has turned into carrying first and taking second, that's the part still moving. Let one thing be handed to you, and let it stay yours.
cells.sheetLine: You carry it well, and you let it be carried back.
cells.verb: holding what the change left standing
cells.place: where you carry weight without going rigid

cells.tense: You are already bracing for a day that hasn't asked anything of you yet.
cells.ask: Pause one full minute before you say yes this week — give the answer after the pause, not before.
cells.core:
You're guarding a calm that might get knocked over, so you're holding tighter than the weight needs. Something that settled recently is getting fenced off as if it were still under threat. You're doing the bearing ahead of time, for a day that hasn't arrived, and the extra grip is showing.

Holding isn't the same as sealing. What has settled stays settled even when you set it down for an hour. The tightening is the part to loosen, not the way you stand. Give the next heavy thing a beat before you take its weight — let the ask finish, then answer.

cells.tense: Some door made you put the load down, and you're still standing in front of it.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, to one person today, that you are carrying something right now.
cells.core:
You still bear weight well. When you pick something up and hold it steady, that works — people hand you shaky things and you don't drop them. That part hasn't gone anywhere. Right now you're at the edge of the work instead of inside it, picking up less than you could hold, and keeping your hands free.

The way back is a direction, not a rest. Pick one thing and move toward it on purpose instead of staying at arm's length from all of it. Say out loud that you're holding it — one sentence, one person, today. Being seen under it is step one.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold more than you're picking up.

cells.tense: You are already keeping things steady for people, and you call it nothing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you agreed to this week and say, in that same breath, that you chose it.
cells.core:
There's a way this goes well: people bring you the shaky things because you don't drop them. You take what's handed over, you keep it level, and the room settles. That's a real thing you do, and it shapes what people say to you and what they trust you with.

The part that's missing is you counting it. The work happens and gets filed as no big deal, so the one doing it doesn't get the credit. When you say you just did it, drop the just. Name one choice out loud, to one person, and let it count as a choice. The say-so is yours to pick up.
cells.sheetLine: Steady isn't a setting. You're doing it.

attempts.check: The record does not say this person's holding was ever tested or that anything in their past actually broke them; Too Little only allows that a moment of bearing weight is being avoided, not what happened there. A reader could reasonably say this is just being a steady person who prefers solid ground, not a capacity with a bend. The asks survive a wrong read because each one is a single visible action — say the number to the second person, take one afternoon off from the guard — and none of them promises a repair. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any line about calm being a form the body has to keep paying for; that is a nice sound, so it goes.
